questions.question: Which is a poor reason to use your horn?

options.text: A driver next to you is too close to the car ahead.
A parked car has someone in the driver's seat.
You want people to look at your motorcycle.
You are passing a person in the street.

questions.correctAnswerText: You want people to look at your motorcycle.
questions.explanation: Use your horn before passing a vehicle or pedestrian who might move into your lane. If a driver next to you is too close to the car ahead, they may try to pass and cut in front of you. If you see someone in a parked car or a pedestrian in the street, sound your horn as you pass.

questions.question: When entering a turn, a rider should:

options.text: Move their shoulders to match the angle of the turn.
Sit up as high as possible.

questions.explanation: Before entering a turn, slow down by releasing the throttle and using the brakes if needed.

questions.question: When riding with a passenger, you should do all of the following, except:

options.text: Avoid talking to the passenger while riding.

questions.correctAnswerText: Avoid talking to the passenger while riding.
questions.explanation: A passenger adds weight, so your motorcycle will respond more slowly. Ride slower than usual, slow down sooner, and keep more distance between you and other vehicles. Always warn your passenger about hazards ahead.

questions.question: When preparing to pass on the left, ride on the left side of your lane because:

options.text: The right side could be slippery.
It gives you the best view of hazards in the next lane.
People don't expect to be passed on their left.
It puts you in the car's rearview mirror.

questions.correctAnswerText: It gives you the best view of hazards in the next lane.
questions.explanation: Ride in the left side of your lane when preparing to pass. This position improves your view ahead and makes you more visible to oncoming traffic.

questions.question: To prevent fatigue on a long ride, you should do all of the following, except:
questions.explanation: Dress to protect yourself from tiring weather like wind and rain. Ride no more than six hours per day and take a break at least once every two hours. Avoid artificial stimulants because you may become extremely tired when they wear off.

questions.question: When braking on a slippery surface, you should:

options.text: Not use brakes, but downshift instead.

questions.explanation: On a slippery surface, reduce your speed and avoid sudden movements. Use both brakes if you need to slow down or stop.

questions.question: In a group ride, inexperienced riders should position themselves:

options.text: Near the back of the group.
At the very end of the group.

questions.explanation: Less experienced riders should ride near the front, just behind the leader. This prevents them from falling behind and allows experienced riders to watch them.

questions.question: Which is not a good safety tip?

options.text: Slow to a safe speed before turning.
Lean in the direction you want to turn.
Avoid dragging your feet on the road.

questions.explanation: Slow down before turning and lean in the direction of the turn. Don't drag your feet on the road, as you could lose control. Always watch for other traffic on the road.

questions.question: A rectangular sign may be a:
questions.explanation: Regulatory signs like speed limits are rectangular with white backgrounds and black letters or symbols. You must follow the rules shown on these signs.

questions.question: A helmet should not:

options.text: Have been worn in a crash.

questions.correctAnswerText: Have been worn in a crash.
questions.explanation: Choose a helmet that meets U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) standards, fits snugly all around, and has no defects. Replace any helmet that was worn during a crash.

questions.question: When another vehicle passes you from behind, where should you ride?

options.text: In the center of your lane.
In the left portion of your lane.
In the right portion of your lane.
In any portion of your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: In the center of your lane.
questions.explanation: Stay in the center of your lane when being passed. This discourages the other driver from moving back into your lane too soon.

questions.question: What does this hand signal mean?

options.text: The group will exit at the next exit.

questions.explanation: When the lead rider raises their left arm and points with one finger, it means the group should form a single-file line.

questions.question: Where should cargo be placed on a motorcycle?

options.text: On one side of the motorcycle.

questions.explanation: Keep cargo low and secure in saddlebags. Placing cargo high on the back changes the motorcycle's balance and raises its center of gravity. Always distribute cargo equally on both sides.

questions.question: When a vehicle passes you on your left, where should you ride?

options.text: Move as far right as possible to help them pass.
Move to the shoulder to help them pass.
Ride in the center of your lane.
Ride in the left portion of your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the center of your lane.
questions.explanation: Stay in the center of your lane when being passed. Riding near the passing vehicle increases collision risk. Riding far from them may tempt them to return to your lane too soon.

questions.question: What happens to a sidecar during acceleration?

options.text: It feels like it is falling behind.
It feels like it is accelerating faster than the motorcycle.

questions.correctAnswerText: It feels like it is falling behind.
questions.explanation: A sidecar is an unpowered weight attached to your motorcycle. Due to inertia, it will feel like it is lagging behind when you accelerate.

questions.question: Which portion of your lane should you ride in before passing another vehicle on the left?
questions.explanation: Ride in the left portion of your lane before passing. This gives you a better view ahead and makes you more visible to oncoming traffic.

questions.question: When looking through a turn, how should you move your head?

options.text: Turn your head and shoulders together.

questions.explanation: Turn only your head to look through the turn. Keep your shoulders and eyes level with the horizon.

questions.question: How often should you check your motorcycle's hydraulic fluid at minimum?
questions.explanation: Check hydraulic fluids and coolants at least once a week. Regular pre-ride inspections help keep your motorcycle safe.

questions.question: When another vehicle is passing you, where should you ride?

options.text: In the left portion of your lane.
In the center of your lane.
In the right portion of your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: In the center of your lane.
questions.explanation: Ride in the center of your lane when being passed. Riding to either side increases risk—it either brings you closer to the passing vehicle or tempts them to return too soon.

questions.question: As weight shifts forward when you brake, what should you do?

options.text: Do nothing. Weight transfer does not affect braking.
Try to lock the front tire.

questions.explanation: As you brake, gradually increase pressure on the front brake lever as the motorcycle's weight moves forward to the front tire.

questions.question: How can you reduce your reaction time?

options.text: Keep your hands ready on the clutch and brakes.
Shift to neutral when slowing down.

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep your hands ready on the clutch and brakes.
questions.explanation: When you approach a dangerous area like an intersection, keep your hands ready on the clutch lever and brakes. This reduces the time you need to react to hazards.

questions.question: How should you load cargo on a motorcycle?

options.text: Put heavier items in front of the tank bag.
Put lighter items near the front.
Avoid placing items over the rear axle.
Place items behind the rear axle.

questions.correctAnswerText: Put heavier items in front of the tank bag.
questions.explanation: Put heavier items in front of the tank bag. Load weight over or in front of the rear axle. Putting weight behind the rear axle makes the motorcycle harder to control.

questions.question: What formation is best for a group of riders going through a curve?
questions.explanation: Staggered formation works well for groups to stay close while giving each rider space. Single-file formation is best when taking curves, turning, or entering or leaving a highway.

questions.question: What is best when riding a three-wheeled motorcycle through a curve?

options.text: Stay in the center of the lane.
Stay on the outside of the lane.

questions.explanation: Three-wheeled motorcycles and motorcycles with sidecars turn differently than two-wheeled motorcycles. The best path through a curve may not follow the curve exactly. You may need to move from the outside to the inside of the curve before straightening out.

questions.question: Is it good to ride on the far side of a lane when following another vehicle?

options.text: Yes, because drivers will see you easily.
No, because drivers rarely check their side mirrors and may not see you.
Yes, because a passenger may tell the driver you are there.
No, because it is illegal to ride anywhere but the center of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: No, because drivers rarely check their side mirrors and may not see you.
questions.explanation: Most drivers check their rearview mirror more often than their side mirrors. When following a car, ride in the center of the lane so the driver is most likely to see you in the rearview mirror.
